B.4 Derivation of TDHF

We now reduce the TDHF operator ℒ𝖬𝖥\mathcal{L}^{\mathsf{MF}} to an operator on matrices ϕ𝒒\phi_{\boldsymbol{q}}. We therefore evaluate

ℒ𝒒MF​ϕ^q=𝒫𝖬𝖥​[h^,ϕ^𝒒]+𝒫𝖬𝖥​[V^,ϕ^𝒒].\mathcal{L}^{\textsf{MF}}_{\boldsymbol{q}}\hat{\phi}_{q}=\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{MF}}[\hat{h},\hat{\phi}_{\boldsymbol{q}}]+\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{MF}}[\hat{V},\hat{\phi}_{\boldsymbol{q}}]. (83)

We interpret Eq. (63) diagramatically: write all Wick contractions diagrams of O^\hat{O} by PP with exactly two dangling legs (so that inserting one more PP would give ⟨O^⟩P\braket{\hat{O}}_{P}). The projector is trivial for the first term, yielding [h^,ϕ^𝒒][\hat{h},\hat{\phi}_{\boldsymbol{q}}]. For the second term there are four non-trivial diagrams for 𝒫𝖬𝖥​V^​ϕ𝒒^\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{MF}}\hat{V}\hat{\phi_{\boldsymbol{q}}}:

The first two are Hartree-like, while the second two are Fock-like (and come with a minus sign). Since ϕ^𝒒\hat{\phi}_{\boldsymbol{q}} acts before V^\hat{V}, there cannot be a PP separating ϕ𝒒\phi_{\boldsymbol{q}} from the interaction vertex. Comparing to the terms above, these diagrams gives

h^H​[P]​ϕ^𝒒+h^H​[ϕ𝒒​P]+h^F​[P]​ϕ^𝒒+h^F​[ϕ𝒒​P].\hat{h}_{H}[P]\hat{\phi}_{\boldsymbol{q}}+\hat{h}_{H}[\phi_{\boldsymbol{q}}P]+\hat{h}_{F}[P]\hat{\phi}_{\boldsymbol{q}}+\hat{h}_{F}[\phi_{\boldsymbol{q}}P]. (84)

Similarly, −𝒫𝖬𝖥​ϕ𝒒^​V^-\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{MF}}\hat{\phi_{\boldsymbol{q}}}\hat{V} gives

−ϕ^𝒒​h^H​[P]−h^H​[P​ϕ𝒒]−ϕ^𝒒​h^F​[P]−h^F​[P​ϕ𝒒].-\hat{\phi}_{\boldsymbol{q}}\hat{h}_{H}[P]-\hat{h}_{H}[P\phi_{\boldsymbol{q}}]-\hat{\phi}_{\boldsymbol{q}}\hat{h}_{F}[P]-\hat{h}_{F}[P\phi_{\boldsymbol{q}}]. (85)

Combining these

𝒫𝖬𝖥​[V^,ϕ𝒒^]=[h^H​[P]+h^F​[P],ϕ^𝒒]+h^H​[[ϕ𝒒,P]]+h^F​[[ϕ𝒒,P]]=[h^H​[P]+h^F​[P],ϕ^𝒒]−h^H​F​[[P,ϕ𝒒]𝒒]\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{MF}}[\hat{V},\hat{\phi_{\boldsymbol{q}}}]=\big[\hat{h}_{H}[P]+\hat{h}_{F}[P],\hat{\phi}_{\boldsymbol{q}}\big]+\hat{h}_{H}\big[[\phi_{\boldsymbol{q}},P]\big]+\hat{h}_{F}\big[[\phi_{\boldsymbol{q}},P]\big]=\big[\hat{h}_{H}[P]+\hat{h}_{F}[P],\hat{\phi}_{\boldsymbol{q}}\big]-\hat{h}_{HF}\big[[P,\phi_{\boldsymbol{q}}]_{\boldsymbol{q}}\big] (86)

The kinetic term 𝒫𝖬𝖥​[h^,ϕ^𝒒]=[h^,ϕ^𝒒]\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{MF}}[\hat{h},\hat{\phi}_{\boldsymbol{q}}]=[\hat{h},\hat{\phi}_{\boldsymbol{q}}] combines with the first term here to give the full (non-boosted) Hartree-Fock Hamiltonian. Altogether then the action of ℒ𝒒MF\mathcal{L}^{\textsf{MF}}_{\boldsymbol{q}} on matrices ϕ𝒒\phi_{\boldsymbol{q}} is

ℒ𝒒MF​ϕq=[hH​F​[P],ϕ𝒒]𝒒−hH​F​[[P,ϕ𝒒]𝒒].\mathcal{L}^{\textsf{MF}}_{\boldsymbol{q}}\phi_{q}=\big[h_{HF}[P],\phi_{\boldsymbol{q}}\big]_{\boldsymbol{q}}-h_{HF}\big[[P,\phi_{\boldsymbol{q}}]_{\boldsymbol{q}}\big]. (87)

The first term is the boosted commutator of the un-boosted HF Hamiltonian, and the second term is (minus) the boosted HF Hamiltonian of the boosted commutator.

Appendix C 2PI Effective Action

While we have focused on extracting the phonon action via Hartree-Fock in the main text, it is worth noting that our procedure is more general. In particular, any approximate scheme for computing the effective action Γ⁡[𝜽]\Gamma[\boldsymbol{\theta}] will do. The existence of such an effective action guarantees that computing for example the kineo-elastic coefficient by first shearing the unit cell, and then boosting, or boosting and the shearing will give the same result. Let us briefly discuss how (Time-dependent) Hartree-Fock can be considered such a scheme. In particular by considering the effective action of the Hamiltonian H⁡[𝜽]H[\boldsymbol{\theta}] as a function of the Green’s function, within the 2PI formalism [104, 76]

Γ⁡[G,𝜽]=i​Tr​log⁡G−1−i​Tr​[G​G0−1​[𝜽]−1]−i​Φ​[G,𝜽]\Gamma[G,\boldsymbol{\theta}]=i\operatorname{Tr}\log G^{-1}-i\operatorname{Tr}[GG_{0}^{-1}[\boldsymbol{\theta}]-1]-i\Phi[G,\boldsymbol{\theta}] (88)

where, G0−1[𝜽]=i∂t−h[𝜽]G_{0}^{-1}[\boldsymbol{\theta}]=i\partial_{t}-h[\boldsymbol{\theta}] is the free propagator and Φ\Phi is the Luttinger-Ward functional, which perturbatively is the sum of all 2 particle irreducible diagrams of the gauge twisted interaction. The effective action in terms of 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta} is obtained by finding the saddle point GG of Γ\Gamma. In particular note that the equation of motion for GG is precisely the usual Dyson equations

0=δ​Γδ​G=i​G−1−i​G0−1+i​Σ​[G]0=\frac{\delta\Gamma}{\delta G}=iG^{-1}-iG_{0}^{-1}+i\Sigma[G] (89)

where Σ⁡[G]=δ​Φ​[G]δ​G\Sigma[G]=\frac{\delta\Phi[G]}{\delta G} is the self energy functional. Hartree-Fock emerges as the lowest order approximation to Φ\Phi in terms of interaction, which in this case is

ΦHF​[G,𝜽]\displaystyle\Phi^{\mathrm{HF}}[G,{\boldsymbol{\theta}}] =12​∫d​𝒓1​d​𝒓2​V​(𝒓1+𝜽⁡(𝒓1,t)−𝒓2−𝜽⁡(𝒓2,t))​Gα​α​(𝒓1,𝒓1)​Gβ​β​(𝒓2,𝒓2)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\int{d}\boldsymbol{r}_{1}{d}\boldsymbol{r}_{2}\,V(\boldsymbol{r}_{1}+\boldsymbol{\theta}(\boldsymbol{r}_{1},t)-\boldsymbol{r}_{2}-\boldsymbol{\theta}(\boldsymbol{r}_{2},t))G_{\alpha\alpha}(\boldsymbol{r}_{1},\boldsymbol{r}_{1})G_{\beta\beta}(\boldsymbol{r}_{2},\boldsymbol{r}_{2}) (90)
−12∫d𝒓1d𝒓2V(𝒓1+𝜽(𝒓1,t)−𝒓2−𝜽(𝒓2,t))Gα​β(𝒓1,𝒓2)Gβ​α(𝒓2,𝒓1)\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\int{d}\boldsymbol{r}_{1}{d}\boldsymbol{r}_{2}\,V(\boldsymbol{r}_{1}+\boldsymbol{\theta}(\boldsymbol{r}_{1},t)-\boldsymbol{r}_{2}-\boldsymbol{\theta}(\boldsymbol{r}_{2},t))G_{\alpha\beta}(\boldsymbol{r}_{1},\boldsymbol{r}_{2})G_{\beta\alpha}(\boldsymbol{r}_{2},\boldsymbol{r}_{1}) (91)

The equations of motion δδ​G​(x,y)​log⁡ZHF=0\frac{\delta}{\delta G(x,y)}\log Z^{\mathrm{HF}}=0 are solved precisely by the solutions to the self-consistent Hartree-Fock problem, with both stationary and time-dependent solutions corresponding to the conventional Hartree-Fock approach, and general time-dependent Hartree-Fock. Making the connection to the variational formulation can be done easily considering multiplying equation (89) with GG, and taking the commutator:

i[∂t,G]=[h+ΣHF[G],G]i[\partial_{t},G]=[h+\Sigma^{\mathrm{HF}}[G],G] (92)

At the Hartree-Fock mean field level, Σ\Sigma becomes local in time, and we recover the most general time-dependent Hartree-Fock equations. By considering stationary solutions [∂t,G]=0[\partial_{t},G]=0, we recover the usual stationary Hartree-Fock equations [h+ΣHF​[G],G]=0[h+\Sigma^{\mathrm{HF}}[G],G]=0. By contrast the linearized TDHF we perform consist of taking a stationary solution G¯\bar{G}, and considering small fluctuations G=G¯+ϕG=\bar{G}+\phi. The linearized equations of motion for ϕ\phi are

i[∂t,ϕ]=[h+ΣHF[G¯],ϕ]+[δ​Σ​[G¯]δ​Gϕ,G¯]=ℒ[ϕ]i[\partial_{t},\phi]=\left[h+\Sigma^{\mathrm{HF}}[\bar{G}],\phi\right]+\left[\frac{\delta\Sigma[\bar{G}]}{\delta G}\phi,\bar{G}\right]=\mathcal{L}[\phi] (93)

which is precisely equation (87). Suppose U=ei​α​AU=e^{i\alpha A} generates a continuous symmetry that commutes with the Hamiltonian, then ϕA=i⁡[A,G¯]\phi_{A}=i[A,\bar{G}] is an exact zero mode of equation (93), which is a manifestation of the Goldstone theorem [45]. Keeping higher order terms in Φ\Phi is a natural extension of HF.
